title: The Garage on Jalan Kusuma Atmaja Where Martha Tilaar Began
dek: Back from Indiana in 1970 with a beautician's licence, Martha Tilaar opened a salon in her father's Jakarta garage on a family loan so that her honest husband would never need to cut corners.

story.event: Opening a beauty salon in her father's garage in Menteng, Jakarta
story.summary: In 1970, after training as a beautician in Bloomington, Indiana, Martha Tilaar opened a salon in the garage of her father's house on Jalan Kusuma Atmaja in Menteng, Jakarta, with Rp 1 million from her father and sister, saying she wanted to improve the finances of her family because her husband, a civil servant, was very honest. The salon soon took over most of the house; a second salon in 1972 introduced traditional herbal treatments, and in 1977 she co-founded PT Martina Berto, maker of Sariayu, which grew into the Martha Tilaar Group.
paragraphs: In the late 1960s Martha Tilaar was in Bloomington, Indiana, where her husband, Alex, was studying on a scholarship that paid him $210 a month and nothing for a wife. She put up hand-drawn flyers offering to babysit for families on campus and, according to a 2003 case study written with her cooperation, was soon looking after 13 children. With the savings she enrolled at the Academy of Beauty Culture, became a state-licensed beautician and offered haircuts door to door. She also sold Avon, and some doors were slammed in her face.

In 1970 the couple came home to Jakarta. Alex was a civil servant and, by her account and the case study's, a very honest one. "My husband is very honest, so I had to improve the finances of our family," she later explained; she did not want him drawn into anything dishonest. With his blessing she turned the garage of her father's house on Jalan Kusuma Atmaja in Menteng, about four metres by six, into a beauty salon. Her father and younger sister put up Rp 1 million. "In fact, I started only with raw courage," she said.

She advertised with brochures handed round from house to house. Her clients were mostly the wives of government officials and foreign ambassadors, the case study says, and within about three months the salon had spread through almost the whole house, leaving the family one small room to live in; another account says it moved to larger premises within six months. In 1972 she opened a second salon, Martha Griya, also in Menteng, where she first offered traditional herbal treatments.

That turn was harder. Jakarta's wealthier women looked to the West for cosmetics, and she was mocked, a 2008 profile said, as if she were a traditional healer gone astray in the city. She kept her fees low for the herbal treatments to bring people in. In 1977, by the company's own history, she founded PT Martina Berto with two partners, one of them a founder of the Kalbe pharmaceutical group, and launched Sariayu. She died in October 2026, aged 89.

quote.text: Never value anything as profitable to thyself which shall compel thee to break thy promise, to lose thy self-respect, to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to act the hypocrite, to desire anything which needs walls and curtains
quote.source_title: Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, tr. George Long, Project Gutenberg eBook #15877
quote.connection: Marcus Aurelius tells himself never to count as profit anything that costs his word or his self-respect. Martha Tilaar opened her salon so that an honest household would not have to face that bargain; the garage and the brochures were the clean way to the money it needed.

reflection: Martha Tilaar's reason for starting was not ambition in the abstract. It was a household sum: what an honest salary covered, and what it did not. Her answer to the gap was to add work of her own, not to ask anyone to bend.

Worry about money can quietly widen what you are willing to do. It may help to name, before you need to, the few things you will not trade for income, and to let that short list shape the work rather than merely fence it in. A garage and a family loan were enough for her to begin.
invitation: Write down one thing you would not do for money in your work, even in a hard month. Put the note where you will see it the next time a tempting shortcut appears.

research_notes: Growth of the first salon: the APEC case (2003, written with her cooperation) says it was extended within three months to fill almost the entire house, leaving the family one small room; detikFinance (2022, citing the company website) says it moved to larger premises within six months; the story gives both. The APEC case also mentions an even earlier small salon in a room of her mother's house in the 1960s, before Indiana; the story treats 1970 as the start, as the company does. Sariayu's origin: the company history, The Jakarta Post (2026), detik and Fortune date PT Martina Berto and Sariayu to 1977, while the APEC case describes a Mustika Ratu partnership with a princess that ended in February 1979, after which she began Sari Ayu as a home industry and later formed the Kalbe joint venture; the Jakarta Post 2008 profile also places Sari Ayu after the end of a partnership with Mooryati Sudibyo. The story attributes the 1977 date to the company's own history. Father's name: Yakob Handana (company) or Handana Tjie (Jakarta Post 2008); the story does not name him. The salon's street (Jl. Kusuma Atmaja) comes from the company history and The Jakarta Post 2026; one Indonesian report says Jl. Tosari, not used. Garage size (about 4 by 6 metres) is from detik citing the company website. The APEC case says she earned up to US$2,000 a month babysitting and bought a car within a month as a beautician; these figures are her own and are not used. The 2008 Jakarta Post profile was written by Ayu Hermawan, who also wrote her authorised biography; it is cited from the Jakarta Jive republication because the Post's 2008 URL was not found. The APEC PDF loads but its text is compressed, so the source checker cannot read the founder's name in it; it was read in full after decompression. Marcus Aurelius's note is advice to himself; the 'walls and curtains' phrase refers to things one would want hidden.
